claims.text: Annealed aluminum has a face-centered cubic crystal structure.
The FCC structure provides multiple slip systems that facilitate dislocation nucleation and mobility during deformation.
The proposed intervention is tensile straining of aluminum in a molecular-dynamics simulation.
The proposed simulations use a temperature of 300 K and strain rates from 10^7 to 10^9 s^-1.
The proposed simulation box is several hundred nanometers in size and is simulated over tens of nanoseconds.
Tensile deformation activates multiple slip systems and efficient dislocation motion in annealed aluminum.
FCC aluminum provides 12 active slip systems.
The availability of 12 active slip systems enables distributed plastic deformation.
Distributed plastic deformation promotes dislocation nucleation and mobility, leading to high ductility under tension.
Under the imposed tensile strain, aluminum will exhibit smooth plastic deformation with widespread dislocation movement and activation of multiple slip systems.
Materials with fewer active slip systems or less favorable dislocation mechanics have lower ductility under similar conditions.
The proposed mechanism applies to annealed aluminum and similar FCC metals at ambient temperature and high strain rates.
High-strain-rate simulation findings may not translate directly to quasi-static experimental strain rates.
Scale effects may alter dislocation behavior.
